covers.quote: Use the form the person uses.
As far as possible, if you need to write a non-English name, use the same form and spelling as the person uses.
As a last resort, use the name that is most commonly used in writing about the person.

rules.quote: When you write to or about people, always use the form of personal name that the person uses.
rules.violation_condition: A person is referred to by a name, spelling or ordering of names that does not match the form they use.
when: Applies both when addressing someone and when writing about them.
For non-English names, use the person's own form and spelling as far as possible.
If the person's own usage cannot be established, use the name most commonly used in writing about them.
The person's preferred name order takes precedence over assumptions based on English-language naming conventions.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: preferred forms, non-English forms and the fallback are cases of the same name-selection check.

rules.quote: ‘given name’ instead of ‘Christian name’
rules.violation_condition: The term ‘Christian name’ is used to refer to a person's given name.
when: Applies when referring to this part of a personal name, rather than discussing or quoting the terminology itself.
rules.why: G-1: retain the specific terminology instruction rather than its general lead-in.

rules.quote: ‘family name’ instead of ‘surname’
rules.violation_condition: The term ‘surname’ is used to refer to a person's family name.
when: Applies when referring to this part of a personal name, rather than discussing or quoting the terminology itself.
rules.why: G-1: retain the specific terminology instruction rather than its general lead-in.

rules.quote: ‘previous names’ instead of ‘maiden name’.
rules.violation_condition: The term ‘maiden name’ is used to refer to a person's previous name.
when: Applies when referring to previous personal names, rather than discussing or quoting the terminology itself.
rules.why: G-1: retain the specific terminology instruction rather than its general lead-in.

covers.quote: Be aware that a few people don’t use capitals for their names. This is a deliberate style decision that is part of their personal identity. Examples include bell hooks and kd lang.
Use the same capitalisation as the person uses.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for the names of real and fictitious people.
rules.violation_condition: A personal name has incorrect initial capitalisation, taking account of the person's own usage and the established capitalisation of any particles.
when: Applies to real and fictitious people's names.
Preserve deliberately non-capitalised personal forms, such as bell hooks and kd lang.
For names containing particles, use the capitalisation the person uses rather than assuming that every particle needs an initial capital.
Sentence-initial particles are covered by the separate sentence-position rule.
Initials and nicknames have their own more specific capitalisation rules.
rules.why: G-1, G-2 and G-4: separate the heading's specific checks, but fold personal and particle-capitalisation exceptions into this check.

rules.quote: Capitalise the initials of people’s given names.
rules.violation_condition: An initial representing a person's given name is lower case.
when: Applies to initials representing given names.
Respect an established personal form that deliberately uses lower case.
rules.why: G-1: initials' capitalisation is a specific check, distinct from their spacing and punctuation.

rules.quote: Write them unspaced and without full stops.
rules.violation_condition: Given-name initials contain full stops or spaces between successive initials.
when: Applies to initials representing given names.
The prohibition on spaces is between initials, not between initials and the family name.
Retain a hyphen that belongs to the person's hyphenated given name.
rules.why: G-2: undotted, unspaced initials are one formatting check; a name's own hyphen is not prohibited punctuation.

rules.quote: Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.
rules.violation_condition: The space joining given-name initials to the family name allows a line break.
when: Applies at the boundary between given-name initials and a family name.
rules.why: G-1: keeping initials attached to the family name is distinct from formatting the initials themselves.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for nicknames.
rules.violation_condition: A nickname is written with incorrect lower-case initials.
when: Applies to nicknames used as personal names.
Respect an established personal form that deliberately uses lower case.
rules.why: G-1: nickname capitalisation and first-use quotation marks are independently flaggable properties.

rules.quote: The first time they appear in your text, place nicknames in quotation marks.
rules.violation_condition: The first occurrence of a nickname in the text is not enclosed in quotation marks.
when: Applies only to the first occurrence of each nickname in the text.
rules.why: G-2: first occurrence is the condition for one quotation-mark check, not a requirement for every occurrence.

rules.quote: The plural of any personal name is formed by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
rules.violation_condition: A personal-name plural has an incorrect ending or changes a final ‘y’ or ‘i’ instead of retaining it.
when: For names ending in ‘s’, ‘x’ or ‘z’, add ‘es’.
For names ending in ‘y’, retain the ‘y’ and add ‘s’.
For names ending in ‘i’, retain the ‘i’ and add ‘s’.
For names ending in ‘o’ or any other letter, add ‘s’.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the table supplies spelling-dependent cases of one plural-formation check.

rules.quote: Punctuate possessive forms with an apostrophe
rules.violation_condition: A personal-name possessive has an incorrect apostrophe or ‘s’ ending, or puts the possessive ending on the wrong member of a coordinated expression.
when: For a singular personal name, add apostrophe ‘s’, including when the name already ends in ‘s’.
For a plural personal name ending in plural ‘s’ or ‘es’, add only an apostrophe.
For the coordinated shared possessive illustrated by ‘Aiko and Tashi’s team’, add apostrophe ‘s’ only to the last name.
For the coordinated pronoun-and-noun construction illustrated by ‘You and your partner’s luggage’, add apostrophe ‘s’ to the noun.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: number and coordination determine the form and location of one possessive ending; the table is not a set of duplicate rules.

rules.quote: Always retain hyphens when you write given and family names that are hyphenated.
rules.violation_condition: A hyphen belonging to a person's given or family name is omitted.
when: Applies when the person's given or family name is hyphenated.
rules.why: G-1: retaining a name's hyphen is distinct from retaining all words of a compound family name.

covers.quote: Keep the compound when writing a person’s family name.

rules.quote: Write all parts of compound family names.
rules.violation_condition: A reference to a person's compound family name omits one or more parts of that compound.
when: Applies to compound family names, including when the given name is omitted.
Distinguish a compound family name from multiple family names where the person is known by only one; the latter has its own first-and-later-mention rule.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: mark compound-name retention once, separately from hyphen retention and the distinct multiple-family-name case.

covers.quote: Sometimes someone has more than one family name but is only known by one.

rules.quote: Write all the names the first time and use the well-known family name after.
rules.violation_condition: A person with multiple family names who is known by only one is introduced without all their names, or later referred to by a family-name form other than the well-known one.
when: Applies when someone has more than one family name but is known by only one.
Use all the names at first mention.
Use the well-known family name in later family-name references.
rules.why: G-2: first and subsequent mentions are conditions of one name-form check.

covers.quote: Keep accents and diacritic marks in names

rules.quote: When you write names, retain diacritic marks unless the person commonly uses a simplified form of their name.
rules.violation_condition: A name omits a diacritic that belongs to its established form, without the person commonly using that simplified form.
when: Applies to diacritics in given and family names.
A simplified form is acceptable when the person commonly uses it.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and G-4: the body states the check and its simplified-form exception; alternative name forms are not violations.

rules.quote: use the same form throughout the content.
rules.violation_condition: A name containing a particle is inconsistently capitalised across the content, other than the required change at the start of a sentence.
when: Applies to the form selected for a name containing a particle when the person cannot be asked.
Do not treat sentence-initial capitalisation of the particle as an inconsistency.
rules.why: G-5: retain the textual consistency requirement, not the source-consultation procedure in the same sentence.

covers.quote: You can also rephrase the sentence to retain the original form.

parts.quote: Willem van Otterloo was chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra.
Van Otterloo was chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra.
The chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra was van Otterloo.

rules.quote: Always use an initial capital for the particle when a name starts a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A name begins a sentence with a lower-case particle.
when: Applies only when the particle itself begins the sentence.
A sentence can be rephrased to put the name elsewhere and retain its original particle capitalisation.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: sentence position triggers the check; rephrasing is an alternative, not a second requirement.

covers.quote: List family name first in reference lists

rules.quote: In a reference list, put the family name first and then the initial for the given name of the lead author.
rules.violation_condition: A reference-list entry gives the lead author's name in an order or form other than family name followed by given-name initials.
when: Applies to the lead author's name in a reference-list entry.
rules.why: G-4: the body gives the more complete reference-name format; the heading is not a second rule.

Sentence-initial particles are covered by the separate sentence-position rule.
Initials and nicknames have their own more specific capitalisation rules.
rules.why: G-1, G-2 and G-4: separate the heading's specific checks, but fold personal and particle-capitalisation exceptions into this check.

anchor.quote: Capitalise the initials of people’s given names.

tags.violation_condition: An initial representing a person's given name is lower case.

when: Applies to initials representing given names.
Respect an established personal form that deliberately uses lower case.
rules.why: G-1: initials' capitalisation is a specific check, distinct from their spacing and punctuation.

anchor.prefix: itials of people’s given names.
anchor.quote: Write them unspaced and without full stops.

tags.violation_condition: Given-name initials contain full stops or spaces between successive initials.

when: Applies to initials representing given names.
The prohibition on spaces is between initials, not between initials and the family name.
Retain a hyphen that belongs to the person's hyphenated given name.
rules.why: G-2: undotted, unspaced initials are one formatting check; a name's own hyphen is not prohibited punctuation.

anchor.prefix: nspaced and without full stops.
anchor.quote: Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.

tags.violation_condition: The space joining given-name initials to the family name allows a line break.

when: Applies at the boundary between given-name initials and a family name.
rules.why: G-1: keeping initials attached to the family name is distinct from formatting the initials themselves.

anchor.quote: Use initial capitals for nicknames.
anchor.suffix: The first time they appear in y

tags.violation_condition: A nickname is written with incorrect lower-case initials.

when: Applies to nicknames used as personal names.
Respect an established personal form that deliberately uses lower case.
rules.why: G-1: nickname capitalisation and first-use quotation marks are independently flaggable properties.

anchor.prefix: initial capitals for nicknames.
anchor.quote: The first time they appear in your text, place nicknames in quotation marks.

tags.violation_condition: The first occurrence of a nickname in the text is not enclosed in quotation marks.

when: Applies only to the first occurrence of each nickname in the text.
rules.why: G-2: first occurrence is the condition for one quotation-mark check, not a requirement for every occurrence.

anchor.quote: The plural of any personal name is formed by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
anchor.suffix: It depends on the spelling of t

covers.quote: Spell plural forms correctly
‘s’, ‘x’ and ‘z’
Add ‘es’
Keep the ‘y’ and add ‘s’
Keep the ‘i’ and add ‘s’
Add an ‘s’
All other letters
Add an ‘s’

parts.quote: There were 3 Yanises and 2 Lizes at the meeting but no Alexes.
The Murphys always meet on Tuesdays.
The 4 young Angelos played together all day.
The 2 Evelyns in the section were cousins.

tags.violation_condition: A personal-name plural has an incorrect ending or changes a final ‘y’ or ‘i’ instead of retaining it.

when: For names ending in ‘s’, ‘x’ or ‘z’, add ‘es’.
For names ending in ‘y’, retain the ‘y’ and add ‘s’.
For names ending in ‘i’, retain the ‘i’ and add ‘s’.
For names ending in ‘o’ or any other letter, add ‘s’.

anchor.quote: Punctuate possessive forms with an apostrophe

covers.quote: Use an apostrophe and an ‘s’ with personal names, even when they already end in ‘s’ (Table 2).
Plural personal names take just an apostrophe. Simply add an apostrophe to the end of the plural form.
Add apostrophe ‘s’ (’s)
Add apostrophe ‘s’ (’s)
Add only an apostrophe (’) without an extra ‘s’
Add only an apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) on the last name
Add only an apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) on the noun

parts.quote: The Joneses’ responses or the Nasrins’ name tags

tags.violation_condition: A personal-name possessive has an incorrect apostrophe or ‘s’ ending, or puts the possessive ending on the wrong member of a coordinated expression.

when: For a singular personal name, add apostrophe ‘s’, including when the name already ends in ‘s’.
For a plural personal name ending in plural ‘s’ or ‘es’, add only an apostrophe.
For the coordinated shared possessive illustrated by ‘Aiko and Tashi’s team’, add apostrophe ‘s’ only to the last name.
For the coordinated pronoun-and-noun construction illustrated by ‘You and your partner’s luggage’, add apostrophe ‘s’ to the noun.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: number and coordination determine the form and location of one possessive ending; the table is not a set of duplicate rules.

anchor.quote: Always retain hyphens when you write given and family names that are hyphenated.

tags.violation_condition: A hyphen belonging to a person's given or family name is omitted.

when: Applies when the person's given or family name is hyphenated.
rules.why: G-1: retaining a name's hyphen is distinct from retaining all words of a compound family name.

anchor.quote: Write all parts of compound family names.

covers.quote: Keep the compound when writing a person’s family name.

tags.violation_condition: A reference to a person's compound family name omits one or more parts of that compound.

when: Applies to compound family names, including when the given name is omitted.
Distinguish a compound family name from multiple family names where the person is known by only one; the latter has its own first-and-later-mention rule.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: mark compound-name retention once, separately from hyphen retention and the distinct multiple-family-name case.

anchor.prefix: name but is only known by one.
anchor.quote: Write all the names the first time and use the well-known family name after.

covers.quote: Sometimes someone has more than one family name but is only known by one.
covers.suffix: Write all the names the first t

tags.violation_condition: A person with multiple family names who is known by only one is introduced without all their names, or later referred to by a family-name form other than the well-known one.

when: Applies when someone has more than one family name but is known by only one.
Use all the names at first mention.
Use the well-known family name in later family-name references.
rules.why: G-2: first and subsequent mentions are conditions of one name-form check.

anchor.quote: When you write names, retain diacritic marks unless the person commonly uses a simplified form of their name.

covers.quote: Keep accents and diacritic marks in names

tags.violation_condition: A name omits a diacritic that belongs to its established form, without the person commonly using that simplified form.

when: Applies to diacritics in given and family names.
A simplified form is acceptable when the person commonly uses it.
rules.why: G-2, G-3 and G-4: the body states the check and its simplified-form exception; alternative name forms are not violations.

anchor.prefix: e on a case-by-case basis, then
anchor.quote: use the same form throughout the content.

tags.violation_condition: A name containing a particle is inconsistently capitalised across the content, other than the required change at the start of a sentence.

when: Applies to the form selected for a name containing a particle when the person cannot be asked.
Do not treat sentence-initial capitalisation of the particle as an inconsistency.
rules.why: G-5: retain the textual consistency requirement, not the source-consultation procedure in the same sentence.

anchor.quote: Always use an initial capital for the particle when a name starts a sentence.

covers.prefix: when a name starts a sentence.

Van Otterloo was chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra.
The chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra was van Otterloo.

tags.violation_condition: A name begins a sentence with a lower-case particle.

when: Applies only when the particle itself begins the sentence.
A sentence can be rephrased to put the name elsewhere and retain its original particle capitalisation.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: sentence position triggers the check; rephrasing is an alternative, not a second requirement.

anchor.quote: In a reference list, put the family name first and then the initial for the given name of the lead author.

covers.quote: List family name first in reference lists

tags.violation_condition: A reference-list entry gives the lead author's name in an order or form other than family name followed by given-name initials.

when: Applies to the lead author's name in a reference-list entry.
rules.why: G-4: the body gives the more complete reference-name format; the heading is not a second rule.

anchor.quote: Names you pronounce the same way but spell differently go together in an alphabetical list.

covers.quote: [In this list, all family names are pronounced ‘Mac’. They are ordered as if they were spelt the same way.]

tags.specification: Read the instruction as including identically pronounced name elements, not only whole homophonic names: the example treats Mac, M’ and Mc as the same prefix, then sorts by the remaining letters.
tags.violation_condition: An alphabetical list separates equivalent name spellings or orders them by their literal spelling instead of treating the equivalent spellings as the same.

when: Applies when personal names are arranged alphabetically.
Treat the equivalent spellings as if they were spelt the same way.
rules.why: G-2 and E-4: equivalent spellings are cases of one sorting check; the example-based interpretation of equivalent prefixes is made explicit.
